user_turns:
My boyfriend went through my phone. Again. A year and a half ago he read my texts with a coworker while I slept, apologized, and we agreed neither of us would go through the other's phone. Sunday I left mine unlocked while I showered, and he scrolled back through eight months of texts with my ex, Felix. He screenshotted some and sent them to himself. On Tuesday he asked me how often I talk to Felix, when he already knew. It was a trap.

Felix and I dated in our twenties and stayed friends, and Andre has known that since our first month. Felix's dad has dementia and went into memory care in April. Felix is an only child and his mom died. Yes, we text most weeks. Nothing in there is sexual and nobody's planning to meet up. He screenshotted a couple of warm things I said to an old friend going through hell, and one time I vented about a fight. That's it.

I think he was looking for something to catch me on. Now he's acting like I'm the one who betrayed him. I'm angry, and I don't feel safe leaving my phone out in my own home. How do I get him to see the phone is the real problem without it blowing up again?

results.result:
The phone is the breach. You already had a rule, he broke it a second time, kept copies, and then asked a question he already knew the answer to so he could catch you being less than complete. Warm texts to an old friend whose father is in memory care do not turn that into your betrayal.

You cannot make him see that. You can say it once, plainly, and refuse to put Felix on trial.

Keep it short and specific. Something like:

"On Sunday you went through eight months of my texts and sent screenshots to yourself. We already agreed we don't go through each other's phones. On Tuesday you asked how often I talk to Felix when you already knew. That was a test. I'm not going to defend a friendship you've known about since our first month. The problem is that you broke the agreement and then set me up. I need you to delete those screenshots, and I need this to stop."

Then stop explaining the texts. The more you justify "nothing sexual" and "nobody's planning to meet," the more the conversation becomes a hearing about whether your friendship was innocent enough to deserve privacy. It was private because you agreed the phone was off limits, not because the messages passed a test.

If he pivots to the fight you vented about, or to how often you text, or to what a "warm" message means, bring it back to one sentence: "I'm talking about you going through my phone." Say it as many times as you need to. You do not owe a line-by-line reading of eight months of messages.

A response that actually takes this in looks like: he deletes what he sent himself, he admits the reading and the trap, and he stops prosecuting the friendship. Anger, defensiveness, or "but look what you said" means he still thinks the search was justified. You already lived that version a year and a half ago, when he apologized and the agreement held until the next unlocked phone.

Locking your phone is reasonable. It will not fix this. You should not have to hide your phone in your own home to keep a promise he already made. If this conversation blows up, that is him choosing the blowup. Your job is to keep the subject on what he did, and then decide what you do if he still treats you as the one who was caught.

Yes. On the facts you described, you are right.

You and Andre already had a rule: neither of you goes through the other's phone. He broke it, kept screenshots, and then asked you a question he already knew the answer to. That is the betrayal in this story.

Texting Felix most weeks, being warm while his dad is in memory care, and venting once about a fight are a friendship Andre has known about since your first month. None of that licensed him to search your phone.

You are also right that he is reversing it. He did something you both forbade, and now he is treating your messages as the offense so he does not have to sit with what he did. Being angry, and not feeling safe leaving your phone out, matches what happened.
